source.title: Penalizing Localized Dirichlet Energies in Low Rank Tensor Products

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The appendix sweeps network width and reports training and test error on MNIST, testing whether test error falls after interpolation with a different study setup than the version’s cited original.
record.gate_note: The paper’s main experiments compare TPBS models with neural networks on tabular datasets; those results do not test the listed versions. The appendix’s MNIST width sweep tests V2. Other generalization claims are background or cited prior work.
record.test_reason: Appendix A directly repeats the width-sweep method and training/test-error measures underlying V2 on MNIST with one-hidden-layer ReLU networks without explicit regularization. AdamW and full-batch updates are recipe differences. This study is not an original source for V2.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes Appendix A: wider interpolating networks have lower test error across all four MNIST training sizes, with faster decay and lower errors for larger datasets. The authors call this partial double descent because the first descent is not observed. The paper's main conclusion concerns localized Dirichlet regularization and TPBS robustness to overfitting and incomplete observations.
record.recipe_differences: The width-sweep setup is close to V2: one-hidden-layer ReLU networks, convergence or zero training error, and no explicit regularization. This study uses full-batch gradient descent with AdamW and tests MNIST; downsampled CIFAR-10 is not tested.
record.method_sensitivity: The rate of test-error decay depends on training-set size; larger datasets show faster decay and lower overall error levels.

fits_no_version.finding: Low-rank tensor-product models can interpolate with exponentially small global Dirichlet energy, motivating localized energy regularization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Global input-gradient Dirichlet energy can be an inadequate complexity penalty for low-rank tensor-product models. This does not test magnitude-aware weight sharpness in convolutional networks.

record.problems: The width-sweep outcomes are presented in a figure without numerical values or uncertainty estimates in the text. The authors call the observed phenomenon partial; they report no first descent because 10 or fewer neurons suffice for interpolation.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the comparison of natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.
Downsampled CIFAR-10 and robustness to other training recipes are not tested.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers, local connectivity, and convolution-derived initialization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, tuning budgets, and optimizer remedies.
Batch-size effects under matched epoch budgets and adaptations that remove their penalty.
Dropout effects, training-set-size dependence, excessive dropout, and removal with weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm or margin measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Partial double descent does not imply partial support for V2: V2 concerns continued improvement beyond interpolation, which the text explicitly reports. The supplied figure extraction does not permit independent numerical verification of monotonicity or the authors' statement that at most ten hidden units suffice for interpolation.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of natural-label and random-label test accuracy.
Tests MNIST only; does not test downsampled CIFAR-10. The text does not identify the exact width at which zero training error begins beyond saying 10 or fewer neurons suffice.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-network comparison.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or comparison of that measure with training-test gaps.
